questions.q: What is the core trade-off of choosing a higher embedding dimensionality?
options: Higher dimensionality always reduces storage cost
Higher dimensionality can capture more semantic nuance, but costs more to store and more to compute similarity over
Higher dimensionality has no effect on storage or compute
Higher dimensionality always slows down training but never affects queries
questions.explain: More dimensions let a model encode finer distinctions in meaning, but every stored vector takes more memory and every similarity computation takes proportionally more compute.

questions.q: Using this lesson's formula (dimensions x 4 bytes), what is the approximate raw storage cost for one 1536-dimension embedding vector?
options: About 1.5 KB
About 60 KB
About 600 bytes
About 6 KB
questions.explain: 1536 dimensions x 4 bytes per float = 6,144 bytes, which is approximately 6 KB, as shown directly in the lesson's worked numbers.

questions.q: Why might a very low-dimensional embedding (e.g., 128 dimensions) hurt retrieval quality?
options: Fewer dimensions means fewer 'slots' to encode distinctions in meaning, which can blur together concepts a higher-dimensional model would keep separate
Low-dimensional embeddings always take longer to compute than high-dimensional ones
Low-dimensional embeddings cannot be stored in any vector database
Low-dimensional embeddings are illegal to use commercially
questions.explain: Dimensionality is a form of representational capacity; too little of it can cause genuinely different meanings to end up represented too similarly, hurting retrieval accuracy.

questions.q: What does Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) allow you to do?
options: Combine two different embedding models into one vector
Store vectors without using any floating-point numbers
Truncate a vector's first N dimensions and still get a coherent, usable embedding, without re-running the model
Automatically translate embeddings between languages
questions.explain: MRL-trained models produce vectors where the leading dimensions are themselves a meaningful embedding, giving a dial to trade quality for storage/speed by truncating rather than re-embedding.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what's the right dimensionality to pick for a real project?
options: Always the smallest dimensionality available, regardless of retrieval quality
Always the largest dimensionality available, regardless of cost
Whatever dimensionality is the current default in the vector database's documentation
The smallest dimensionality that still gives acceptable retrieval quality for your specific content and queries
questions.explain: The lesson frames this explicitly as a quality-vs-cost trade-off, with the right answer being the smallest size that still retrieves well for your actual data, not simply the smallest or largest option available.
